en: Homage to the five glorious gurus. Homage to the glorious Candraprabha.
Composed by the King of Sages, the glorious Indranandin:
The Śrī Jvālāmālinī Kalpa.
The First Chapter, together with the Vernacular Commentary and the Mantra-Tantra. // Auspicious Invocation //
I pay homage to the Lord of Jinas, Candraprabha, whose majesty brings joy to Indra like that of the moon, and whose two lotus-feet are worshipped by Jvālāmālinī. //1//

May the goddess Vahni protect me—she whose limbs are as white as the petals of a night-lotus, who is radiant with brilliant ornaments and mounted upon a great buffalo, her body formidable with garlands of flames. // 2 //
Victory to the Goddess Jvālāmālinī, who rises with a trident, noose, goad, bow, arrow, fruit, and the gesture of granting boons; she is radiant with eight arms marked by the discus. // 3 //
Having prostrated again and again before the Arhats, Siddhas, Ācāryas, and Upādhyāyas, as well as all the foremost of holy sages, I shall now expound the *Jvālanīkalpa*.
In the southern region, in the village of Hemagrāma on Mount Malaya, there was a great-souled sage named Helācārya, a wise master of the Draviḍagaṇa. // 5 //
The reason for composing this work—
the story of Kamalaśrī:
Her disciple Kamalaśrī, or Śrutadevī, was a knower of all the scriptures.
She was seized by a brahmarākṣasa due to the power of her fierce karma. // 6 //
At twilight, he weeps with cries of "Alas! Alas!", spreads a loud, boisterous laughter, chants and recites the Vedas, and then laughs again with the sound of "Kaha Kaha."
"Who is that minister who dwells here, who might liberate me by the power of his own mantra?
He speaks with arrogance and brings about a decay characterized by agitation. (8)
Seeing her thus afflicted by that evil spirit, the Lord of Sages became agitated, bewildered as to what ought to be done to counteract it. // 9 //

For the sake of liberating him from that seizure, the preeminent sage, according to the prescribed rite, propitiated the gods and the fire-god on the peak of the Blue Mountain near that place of seizure.
After seven days, the Goddess, having become manifest and standing before him, said to the sage, "O Noble One, tell me, what is your task? The sage spoke thus: (11)

"For you were detained for the sake of sensual pleasure, in order to achieve results pertaining to this world; however, I have detained you for the sake of releasing Kamalaśrī from her captivity. Therefore, O Goddess, grant release from that captivity—this alone is my purpose."
Having heard those words, she said: "How insignificant is this! (13)
"Do not harbor distress in your mind; be liberated by this mantra," he said, and gave him an exceedingly soft iron leaf upon which the mantra was inscribed.
Not knowing the ritual procedure for that mantra, the sages spoke again to the Goddess:
"Do not withhold anything from us; bestow it upon us. (15)
To him, she then explained that reality along with its instructions;
and now, out of devotion for him, I likewise grant that perfected knowledge. (16)

O Yamī, by means of the ritual procedure for accomplishment, you shall grant success even to one devoid of fire-offerings and recitation; however, this knowledge shall not be granted here again to one who does not give [the required offering].
Standing in a delightful garden grove, in a temple of the Jina, on the bank of a river, on a sandbank, or on another mountain peak— in a place free from living beings— // 18 //

Having thus instructed [the disciple] and performed the fire-oblation (homa) while remaining in that state, let him perform the preliminary service (pūrvasevā); having spoken thus, she returned to her own abode. // 19 //
Remaining right there,
he then meditated upon that wicked one who was being consumed by the syllables of fire, and he expelled him.
If the planet is to be expelled, let it go alone; [use] the seed-syllable *ra-ra-ra-ra* like the earth and fire.
What remains of the ten methods of subjugation (*nigraha*)? Is there any planet at all that can be accomplished? // 21 //
The lineage of the author's gurus is as follows: by the command of the Goddess, that scripture is the Jvālinīmata;
its disciples were Gāṅgamuni, Nīlagrīva, and Vijābja. (22)
All the wives of the brothers-in-law, as well as the young girls, having said "So be it," departed according to the sequence of seniority or by way of their respective lineages. 23.
Kandarpa learned it from him as well; he, in turn, explained that [teaching] along with its instructions to the venerable sage Guṇanandin, who was free from all distinctions.

Between those two [treatises], that scripture was also specifically and correctly proclaimed in its entirety, both in terms of its textual composition and its meaning, by the Sage named Indranandi. (25)
Keeping in mind that the previous treatise was defiled and bound by knots, that sage Indranandin composed [this work] in the form of graceful Āryā verses, songs, and other such compositions. (26)

Listen to this work, composed by the venerable teacher through the turning back of the scriptures for a sublime purpose; it brings benefit to the people of the world and is a singular marvel to the entire universe. // 27 //
The author's table of contents:

the seal of the minister-graha, the mandala, the mustard-oil [rite], the yantra, the subjugation (vaśya), the sutra-tantra, the procedure for bathing, the procedure for the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and then the procedure for accomplishment (sādhana). // 28 //
Based on their respective authorities, I shall clearly explain in brief the description of the essential nature of these ten conscious selves, just as it was taught by the Goddess. (29)
The characteristics of a minister:
one who is silent, of restrained mind, intelligent, capable of piercing the seed-syllable, and free from illusion, intoxication, and pride—such a minister succeeds, without a doubt. (30)
One who is purified by right vision, devoted to the worship of the Goddess, endowed with vows,
intent upon the recitation of mantras and fire-offerings, and free from indolence— such a person is known as a true practitioner of mantra (mantrin).

The mantra-practitioner should be devoted to the gods, the guru, and the samaya; possessed of discernment, truthful in speech, and skillful; eloquent, with semen under control, pure, and fierce-minded. (32)

He who is devoted to the pair of feet of the Goddess, endowed with devotion to the lotus feet of the lineage of the Helā-Ācāryas, and proceeds according to the path taught by his own guru—he shall be a true practitioner of mantra (mantrī). // 33 //
The Goddess indeed bestows contentment and nourishment upon one whose mind is endowed with devotion to the Guru of the Vidyā;
however, toward a mind devoid of devotion to the Guru of the Vidyā, she is exceedingly hostile.

One who is far from right vision, whose speech is confused, who follows the Vedic meters [only for show], who is full of deceit, whose heart is empty, and who is shameless—such a person should not be a minister in this scripture. (35)

Thus ends the section on the characteristics of the mantra, from the *Jvālāmālinīkalpa* composed by the venerable Indranandimuni based on the meaning expounded by Ācārya Helā, with the commentary (*bhāṣā-ṭīkā*) composed by Ācārya Candraśekhara Śāstrī.
The first chapter is completed. The second chapter: the causes for the seizing of the planets.
On this earth, houses seize a man who is excessively joyful in mind, dejected, bound by intense affection or enmity, terrified, or whose mind is distracted elsewhere. // 1 //

The planets seize [the native] out of a desire for pleasure, a desire for tribute, or a desire to destroy; others seize them out of enmity with a desire to kill, or for various remaining reasons. // 2 //
Furthermore, planets are of two kinds according to their classification: by the distinction between divine and non-divine planets.
Divine planets are also of two kinds, by the distinction between male and female planets. (3)
A male spirit does not seize a man when a female spirit has arisen, nor does a female spirit seize a woman; however, a male spirit seizes a woman, and a female spirit seizes a man. // 4 //
This rule regarding the seizing of the *Ratikāma* [planet] has been declared; there is no such restriction elsewhere.
A male house seizes a man, and a female house seizes women. (5)
The characteristics of the divine male spirits (puruṣagraha):
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, brahmarākṣasas, bhūtas, and those called vyantaras—these are the seven male spirits. // 6 //
The god is pure everywhere; the naga lies down and crushes every limb;
the yakṣa drinks milk constantly and weeps and laughs in many ways. // 7 //
At twilight, the Gandharva sings with a beautiful voice, as does the Rākṣasa who is devoted to sacred knowledge; he conquers, recites the Vedas, is attached to women, and is full of pride. (8)
He dilates his eyes, moves with partial gait, yawns, and stretches;
he becomes possessed, faints, weeps, and runs about; eating much, such a Vyantara likewise falls to the ground.
Thus have I fully described the characteristics of the houses of divine men;
now the characteristics of the houses of divine women are being explained—listen! (10)
The divine female spirits (divya-strī-graha) and their characteristics:
Kālī, Karālī, Kaṅkāli, Kālarākṣasī, Jaṅghī, Pretāśinī, Yakṣī, Vaitālī, and Kṣetravāsinī. // 11 //
The body becomes black and the heart, hands, and eyes are consumed by fire; even at night, one afflicted by Karālikā does not consume food.

The face becomes pale, the limbs emaciated, and a blackish discoloration spreads over the body; seized by this [demoness], he wanders at night. Afflicted by the Rākṣasī, he utters loud, mocking laughter at the weaver.
One seized by Jaṅghī faints and weeps, and the body becomes emaciated; one seized by Pretāśinī becomes startled or terrified by the sound of her terrifying voice.
If that same hero rises with his lips bitten, it is declared by the wise to be the "graha" (seizure);
beyond two months, there is no medical treatment for him in this world.
O banyan tree, this yakṣī does not allow you to eat, nor does she permit union with her beloved wife; she lives secretly by herself and will not tolerate [your presence]. 16.
The mouth becomes parched and the body emaciated; the Vaitālika spirits seize him.
Afflicted by the deity dwelling in that field, the man dances and laughs "ha, ha. (17)
She assumes an entrance resembling lightning, speaks in the Kaulika tongue, and runs with great speed; this is declared to be the true characteristic of the female spirit possession.
Likewise, there exist others who hold false views; the wise, by means of their power, transform even those into holders of truth. (19)

This Kaulika [system] of the Bhūtas and Devas is seen through the mutual transposition of the letters a, ka, kha, ga, gha, ja, as well as ta, pa, ya, śa, ra, ṣa, la, sa, la, kṣa, va, ha, ra, and la, when joined with the letter *ra*.
The non-divine planetary seizures (grahas) are named Aṃśukalā, Mādana, Graha, Śākhila, Śaśa, and Nāga;
the six apasmāra-grahas are said to be those that emerge from the breaking of the neck. // 21 //
Those celestial grahas indeed do not release [their victim] without merit;
their mantras are to be accomplished in the tantra, and furthermore, they are applied in meditation. // 22 //

Thus [ends] the commentary on the meaning of the *Jvālāmālinīkalpa*, a poetic work composed by the venerable Indranandimuni, as expounded by the illustrious Helācārya; prepared by Tīrthācārya Prācyavidyāvāridhi Śrī Candraśekhara Śāstrī.
In the Bhāṣā-ṭīkā, the second chapter, titled "The Section on Divine and Non-Divine Planets," is completed. // 2 //
The third chapter:
the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa;
for without sakalīkaraṇa, the mantra-practitioner [is unable to perform] the rites of subjugation and so forth, such as the rites of immobilization.
Since [the practitioner] is incapable [of that], I shall first explain the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of complete identification). // 1 //
Having placed the seed-syllables vaṃ, maṃ, haṃ, saṃ, and likewise taṃ upon the joints of the fingers of both hands, one should thereafter perform the purification of all limbs with them. // 2 //
One should place the syllables *raṃ*, *rīṃ*, *rūṃ*, *rauṃ*, *raḥ* on the joints of the fingers of the left hand, and the seed-syllable *raṃ*;
furthermore, one should likewise place these [other] syllables—*hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *hraṃ*, *hraiḥ*, *hraḥ*—in the same manner. // 3 //

O Goddess, having placed these very limbs—Vāmā and the others—upon the two feet, the hips, the belly, the face, and the head, one should assign them along with Svāhā to the five parts of one's own body. //4//
[Mantra:
Oṃ vaṃ rāṃ hrīṃ Jvālāmālinī, protect my two feet, svāhā!
Oṃ maṃ rīṃ hrīṃ Jvālāmālinī, protect my hips, svāhā!
Oṃ haṃ rūṃ hrūṃ Jvālāmālinī, protect my belly, svāhā!
Oṃ saṃ rauṃ hrauṃ Jvālāmālinī, protect my face, svāhā!
Oṃ taṃ raḥ hraḥ Jvālāmālinī, protect my head, svāhā!
One should meditate upon oneself as blazing intensely from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head;
by this, malevolent spirits, serpents, *śākinīs*, and wicked beasts are destroyed upon being pierced through.

One should place *kṣaṃ*, *kṣīṃ*, *kṣūṃ*, *kṣeṃ*, *kṣaiṃ*, *kṣoṃ*, *kṣauṃ*, *kṣaṃ*, and *kṣaḥ* in the directions starting from the east; this constitutes the binding of the directions from the base up to the sky. // 6 //
The wise one should meditate upon himself as a yellow, indestructible vajra-fortress, square on all sides and impenetrable by others—this is the stronghold. (7)
At the time of mantra recitation and fire offerings, no malevolent planet, even one seeking to kill, can harm the skilled practitioner who has entered the midst of the fortress.
In the seven bhūtis, three bhūs should be drawn according to the prescribed rule, with all their compartments facing every direction,
measuring forty-nine squares.
The expansion of these nine words is now described: one should write the nine principles, each in its own place, according to the prescribed order within the nine squares of the *piṇḍī*.
Then, using groups of three and four squares at its corners, one should arrange twelve *piṇḍas* in a clockwise direction. (10)

In this eighth section, twelve types of ritual cakes (piṇḍa) shaped like eyes, beginning with the piṇḍa, will be described, as well as the suppression of the planets for the purpose of paralyzing [enemies] and other such rites. // 11 //
*Kṣalvyrūṃ, hlavyrūṃ, bhalvyrūṃ, malvyrūṃ, yalvyrūṃ, palvṛyrūṃ, dhalvyrūṃ, jalvyrūṃ, khalbyrūṃ, chamlvyrūṃ, chamlvryūṃ, kalvyrūṃ,
kamlvyrūṃ.* And one should write Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā,
Sañjambhā, Mohā, Gaurī, Gāndhārī, Cakrī, Blūṃ, and those beginning with Oṃ on the sides. (12)
One should write "svāhā" at the end [of the mantras], "kṣīṃ klīṃ" at the sides, and "hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hraḥ" in the four squares;
then, one should draw vajras at the tips of the lines and in all the remaining spaces—this is declared to be the Vajrapañjara.
The specific ritual procedure for each of the divine Mothers regarding the rice-balls (piṇḍas) shall be written down separately;
a woman should not enter among them at all with the central rice-ball.

One should draw a protective Yantra consisting of a lotus with eight petals upon a frame of thorny Kharakeśara; on the outer petals, one should sequentially write the eight Mothers, beginning with Brāhmaṇī and ending with Brahmāṇī, followed by the word "Namaḥ."

The practitioner of mantra should write the eight syllables *pa-ra-gha-u-ṣa-cha-ṭha-va-piṃ* as separate clusters in sequence; likewise, he should write the nine principles beginning with *gra-na-vā-dy-ā-nava*, ending with *namaḥ*. (16)
One should write "Kroṃ" at the tips of all the petals and "Hrīṃ" within the spaces between all the petals;
then, one should encircle the exterior with the mantra: "Oṃ nava tattvaṃ jvālinī namaḥ. // 17 //

"Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ drāṃ drīṃ hrāṃ āṃ kroṃ kṣīṃ, salutation to Jvālāmālinī. Thus has been stated this supreme root mantra of Jvālinī; while reciting it, one should meditate upon the Goddess in its midst, surrounded by her eight Mothers. 18.
In order to describe the meditation upon the true form of the goddess Jvālāmālinī,
they describe [the Lord] Candraprabha, the Lord of Jinas, who possesses the splendor of the moon and delights Indra.
Wearing [the jewel] upon his head with devotion, it shines through the crest of his diadem. // 19 //
Her limbs are as white as the petals of a night-lotus; she is mounted upon a buffalo, adorned with brilliantly shining ornaments;
O Śrījvālinī, you have three eyes, and your body is formidable with garlands of flames. // 20 //
Holding in her hands a noose, a trident, a bow, a plow, a discus, and the gift of excellent fruit—the meritorious eighth mistress of the yakṣas. 21.
One should write the syllable *śrīmat*, the goad (*kāṅkuśa*), and the peak (*kūṭa*) joined with *hari* (the letter *ha*) and the nasal dot (*bindu*).
Then one should write the arrows (*bāṇa*) consisting of twelve phonemes together with the Mothers (*mātṛ*), conjoined with four zeros (*śūnya*).
Entering the interior of the excellent Vajra-pañjara cage, one becomes unassailable by the wicked;
one shall utterly expel the Śākinīs and other great malevolent grahas. // 22 //

"Śrīmat āṃ krau ī kṣāṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ kṣalvvyrūṃ, hlavyrūṃ, bhalvyrūṃ, malvyrūṃ, yalvyrūṃ, palvṛyrūṃ, dhalvyrūṃ, jalvyrūṃ, khalbyrūṃ, chamlvyrūṃ, chamlvryūṃ, kalvyrūṃ, kamlvyrūṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣoṃ kṣaḥ. If, after setting down the vessel, the practitioner, considering it to be an offering (bali), goes toward his home, he should nevertheless establish a bond of hope there; in this way, [the obstacle] truly departs. // 23 //

Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hrauṃ hraḥ Jvālinī! Protect the two feet, the hips, the belly, the face, and the head; having thus heated the five parts of the other's body at the conclusion of the fire offering (homānta). // 24 //

Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hrauṃ hraḥ, protect, protect the feet, the hips, the belly, the mouth, and the head of the vessel of Jvālāmālinī, svāhā! [This is done] with the seed-syllables ending in *ū*—*gra*, *ha*, *ni*, *dha*, *kṣa*, *ha*, *bha*, *ma*, *ya*, *ra*—preceded by the letter *pū* (the letter *p*) joined with the full moon (*o*). These are the poisonless seeds.
With the two enemy-seeds (the *ṛ* and *ṝ* vowels) joined with the bindu, the upper *repha*, and the syllables *mala-vara-yūṃ*. // 25 //

One may perform the rites of immobilization, paralyzing, striking, crushing, dispatching, burning, piercing, binding, breaking the neck, severing limbs, killing, and nourishing for the sake of the planetary spirits (grahas). // 26 //
From laughter comes the void of cessation (*nirodha-śūnya*); the second, fourth, and sixth vowels;
the syllable *oṃ* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*), and the visarga—these are the five kalās.
Oṃ! The five peaks (kūṭa) joined with the five vowels, the pentad of peaks together with cessation;
the mantra for the suppression of evil planets and likewise the two pillars: phaṭ phaṭ ghe ghe. 28.
Oṃ kṣalvyrūṃ Jvālāmālini! Hrīṃ, Klīṃ, Blūṃ, Drāṃ, Drīṃ, Kṣāṃ, Kṣīṃ, Kṣūṃ, Kṣauṃ, Kṣaḥ, Hāḥ! Paralyze the wicked grahas! Hāṃ, Āṃ, Kroṃ, Kṣīṃ! Jvālāmālinī commands: Huṃ Phaṭ Phaṭ! Ghe Ghe!
Oṃ! The mantra for paralyzing (stobhana) consists of the syllable *śūnya* (the void), the *piṇḍa*, the five vowels, the seed-syllable *ha*, and the five [consonants], together with *nirodha*.
It summons all the grahas: [the mantra is] *dvayaṃ saṃvauṣaṭ*. (29)

Oṃ halvyrūṃ jvālāmālini hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ drāṃ droṃ gvīṃ hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ hauṃ haḥ hāḥ! Paralyze all evil planetary spirits (duṣṭagrahān) with *stobhaya* twice; summon them with *ākarṣaya* twice! Hāṃ āṃ koṃ kṣīṃ! Jvālāmālinī commands: *saṃvauṣaṭ*. *Bhaktibha piṇḍo*, *bhrāṃ*, *bhrīṃ*, *bhrauṃ*, *bhraḥ*, together with *sannirodha*. Crush and strike the evil planetary spirits: *matha tāḍaya hūṃ phaṭ ghe ghe*. This is the mantra for striking (*tāḍanamantra*). // 30 //

Oṃ bhalvyrūṃ jvālāmālinī hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ drāṃ drīṃ bhrāṃ bhrīṃ bhrūṃ bhrauṃ bhraḥ hāḥ! Strike the evil planets twice! Hāṃ, Āṃ, Kroṃ, Kṣīṃ! Jvālāmālinī commands: Huṃ phaṭ twice! Ghe ghe! The *mapiṇḍa* for subduing and so forth is: mrāṃ mrīṃ mrūṃ mrauṃ mraḥ; likewise, the restraint is: huṃ phaṭ ghe ghe, using the names of all the *grahas* with a vajra-made needle. (31)
"Visphoṭaya akṣīṇi dvi tathāiva hūṃ phaṭ ghe ghe.
This is the mantra for splitting the eyes; its mudrā is named Akṣibhañjinī (the Eye-breaker). // 32 //

Oṃ malvyrūṃ jvālāmālinī hrīṃ krīṃ blūṃ drāṃ grīṃ mrāṃ mrīṃ mrauṃ mraḥ! Drive away the evil planets, hūṃ phaṭ! With a vajra-made needle, pierce, pierce the eyes of all evil planets, hāṃ āṃ kroṃ kṣīṃ! Jvālāmālinī commands: huṃ phaṭ ghe ghe! Bhaktyādi, vāyupiṇḍa, ya ya ya ya yāḥ yāḥ! Now, dispatch all the planets, ghe ghe huṃ jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ! This is the excellent mantra for dispatching [the spirits]. // 33 //
Oṃ yalvyrūṃ jvālāmālini hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ drāṃ drīṃ ** ya ya ya yāḥ! Drive away all evil planetary spirits (duṣṭagraha)! Ghe ghe hāṃ āṃ kroṃ krīṃ! Jvālāmālinī commands: huṃ jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ!
Vāmādi-ragnipiṇḍa śihki maddevī jvala dva yaṃ ra ra ra ra rāṃ rāṃ! Blaze up! huṃ! Dhagayuga dhūṃ dhūṃ! O Dhūmāndhakāriṇī, you whose crest is a flame! // 34 //
The gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, brahmarākṣasas, and bhūtas—those hundreds of millions of deities and thousands of millions of piśāca kings. // 35 //
"Further, further! At every step, O Ghe, shatter and slay!"—this pair [of mantras] is also [included].
"O you with burning eyes, bring about dissolution! O you whose mouth emits 'dhagaddhag'! O Flaming One! Hrāṃ Hrīṃ! (36)
Hrūṃ hrauṃ hraḥ, O heart of all seizing spirits! Hūṃ! Burn, burn! These are the words of the mantra. Ha ha ha ha hāḥ hāḥ phaṭ ghe ghe—this is the homa mantra. (37)

Oṃ ralbthrūṃ jvālāmālini hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ drāṃ drīṃ jvala jvala ra ra ra ra rāṃ rāṃ jvala prajvala prajvala huṃ huṃ dhaga dhaga dhū dhū dhūmāṃdhakāriṇi jvalanśikhe! Burn the gods! Burn the nāgas! Burn the yakṣas! Burn the gandharvas! Burn the brahmarākṣasas! Burn the bhūtas and grahas! Burn the vyantara grahas! Burn all evil grahas! Burn, burn the hundred million deities!

"Burn, burn the thousand billion kings of the piśācas! Burn, burn the hundred thousand billion apasmāra-grahas! Ghe ghe! Sphoṭaya sphoṭaya! Māraya māraya! O you with burning eyes, O you whose mouth is crackling with destruction, O you garlanded in flames! Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hrauṃ hraḥ! The heart of all wicked grahas: huṃ! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Cut, cut! Split, split! Ha ha ha ha hāḥ hāḥ! Āṃ kroṃ kṣīṃ! Jvālāmālinī commands: huṃ phaṭ ghe ghe!
[One should offer] into the triangular fire-pit (agni-kuṇḍa) the three sweets, all grains, and all salts.
A wise person should perform the fire-oblation with wood from the rājapalāśa and śamī trees. // 38 //
Having recited the *bhūḥ-khyā-gāyatrī* three times or once, one should kindle the fire;
one should perform the kindling of the fire three times at the beginning of each daily ritual.
“Oṃ, we meditate upon the Vajra-snout; we meditate upon the Single-tusked one; may the nectar of speech arise; may that [mantra] of ours impel us.
The syllable *gha*—joined with the *praṇava* (oṃ), the *nagha-piṇḍa*, the five kalās, and the *repha* (the letter *r*) at its base—is the obstruction.
With the true vidyā of the sword-syllables *ghaṃ ghaṃ khaṃ khaṃ khaḥ*, O Rāvaṇa, strike down the mace-wielder! 40.
"By means of the moon-like smile of truth, cut twice, split twice: *ūṃ ūṃ khaṃ khaṃ haṃ saṃ phaṭ phaṭ ghe ghe maṃ*. This mantra, when recited as *jaṭha*, shall be a piercer. // 41 //

*Bhalbyrūṃ*, O Jvālāmālinī! *Hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *blūṃ*, *drāṃ*, *drīṃ*, *ghrāṃ*, *ghrīṃ*, *ghrūṃ*, *ghrauṃ*, *ghraḥ*, *hāḥ*, *ghaṃ*, *ghaṃ*, *khaṃ*, *khaṃ*! "Hāḥ! Together with the full moon"—this is the mantra for seizing the fist. // 42 //
"Oṃ jalvyrūṃ jvālāmālini hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ drāṃ drīṃ hājaḥ.

Without the *piṇḍa*, [the mantra] is "hā phaṭ ghe ghe. With this mantra, the true practitioner of mantras should effect the transfer of the planetary influence (*grahasaṃkrāma*) there and elsewhere by means of the release of the fist. 43.

"Hāḥ phaṭ ghe ghe"—this is the *piṇḍa* mantra; it is the restraint accompanied by the five principles beginning with discipline (*vinaya*). Perform the subjugation of all those named as planets, likewise with "hraṃ phaṭ ghe ghe. (44)

Oṃ jhalvyrūṃ jvālāmālini hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ drāṃ drīṃ jhrāṃ jhrīṃ jhra jhrauṃ jhraḥ hāḥ! Paralyze, paralyze all evil planetary spirits (grahas)! Strike them twice! Shatter their eyes twice! Drive them away twice! Break them apart twice! Hāḥ hāḥ hāḥ! Āṃ kroṃ kṣīṃ! Jvālāmālinī commands: Huṃ phaṭ ghe ghe!
Oṃ! The syllable *kānta* (ka), the *piṇḍa* (na), joined with the five vowels (*pañcasvara*), together with the *tala* (ra) and the letter *pa*;
followed by *hāḥ phaṭ ghe*: O you who shatter the throats of all planetary spirits, perform this twice! Ghe ghe! (Verse 45)

Oṃ khalvyrūṃ jvālāmālini hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ drāṃ drīṃ khrāṃ khrīṃ khraṃ khrauṃ khraḥ hāḥ phaṭ ghe ghe! Cause the throat and limbs of all the *grahas* to be bound! Hāṃ āṃ kroṃ kṣīṃ! Jvālāmālinī commands: huṃ phaṭ ghe ghe! The *piṇḍa-mantra* begins with *bhakti* and ends with *ca*; it consists of five syllables joined with the letter *repha* (*r*), ending in *nirodha*.
For the names of all the *grahas*, [the mantra is]: "cut! phaṭ phaṭ ghe ghe! // 46 //

Oṃ chamlvyrūṃ jvālāmālini hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ drāṃ drīṃ chrāṃ chrīṃ chraṃ chrauṃ chraḥ hāḥ! By the name of all the *grahas*, sever, sever the mantras! Hāṃ āṃ kroṃ kṣīṃ! Jvālāmālinī commands: huṃ phaṭ ghe ghe!
O you who possess the lunar orb together with devotion, *blīṃhāḥ*, strike, strike all the seizing spirits (*graha*) with the six [weapons];
cast them down upon the ground, *hūṃ* twice, *phaṭ* twice, *ghe ghe*. 47.

Oṃ ṭhalvryūṃ Jvālāmālini hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ drāṃ drīṃ blīṃ hāḥ! Strike all evil planetary spirits with thunderbolts of stone! Cast them down upon the earth! Hāṃ āṃ kroṃ kṣīṃ! Jvālāmālinī commands: huṃ phaṭ ghe ghe!
The very essence of the Vinaya is its fivefold reality; [perform] the cessation of all those named as planets. Subdue them all! Su phaṭ ghe ghe! 48.

Burn them! Split them! Bind them! Break their necks! Cut their entrails, cut them! Kill them! Hāṃ āṃ kroṃ kṣīṃ! Jvālāmālinī commands: huṃ phaṭ ghe ghe!
Subdue them; render them poisonless; [reduce them to] a lump; [subject them to] their own five elements along with suppression.
Submerge all the seizing spirits twice in the ocean: *hūṃ*, likewise *phaṭ phaṭ ghe ghe*! // 49 //

JHABHLVYRŪṂ JVĀLĀMĀLINI HRĪṂ JHĪṂ BLŪṂ DRĀṂ DRĪṂ SAṂ TAṂ VAṂ MAṂ HAṂ ŪṂ! O Jvālāmālinī, rouse all evil planetary spirits! Make them dance! Make them dance! HĀṂ ĀṂ KROṂ HRĪṂ! Having consecrated water with unbroken rice grains using this mantra for the purpose of suppressing and nourishing all [obstacles], one should strike [the patient] and wash [them]; thus the subjugation is accomplished. // 51 //

Whether it be the self, another, a reflected image, or a formal debate that is established, the seizing and subduing [of the opponent] occurs; such is the true doctrine of the Goddess who dwells upon the peak. 52.

Having wrapped each syllable individually around a slender tube made of *īṣanātra* grass, one should recite [the mantra] two hundred and seven times with these beads at the three junctions of the day. (53)

All poisons of venomous serpents, poisons of malevolent *śākinīs*, poisons of malevolent planetary spirits (*graha*), and poisons of malevolent humans shall become poisonless; they shall come under one's control, and the world shall be shaken. (54)
Just as horses and elephants are urged by the wise with words, whips, hooks, and their feet,
so too do all beings, both divine and non-divine, dance in accordance with the awakening call.
Having pierced the heart and ears of the evil planet with sharp and excellent mantras, let the wise one perform whatever task he intends upon this earth. (56)
The significance of the seed-syllable (bījākṣara) as gnosis and its ritual application have not been fully explained here; they are all described in the Gāruḍa scriptures.
Having attained that distinction, whatever word the practitioner of mantras (mantrī) utters, that indeed shall be the mantra. (57)
If the practitioner should raise an objection, let him speak it to the Jina himself;
having reflected upon my words, whatever word he speaks shall be the mantra. (58)

Having spoken to the Lord of the Side (Pārśvajina) regarding cutting, burning, sending forth, piercing, striking, firm binding, weakening, or anything else, whatever word one utters shall be a mantra. (59)

Having understood what is divine and non-divine, what is achievable and unachievable, what is to be awakened and what is not to be awakened, and having known the seed-syllable and the non-seed-syllable—the very word that one speaks shall be the mantra. (60)
Even while reciting the words of a mantra with knitted brows, bloodshot eyes, terrifying laughter, and cries of "hā hā," whatever word one utters shall itself be the mantra. // 61 //
Whatever the enemy desires that is not to be challenged, he brings that very thing to pass; for the seed-syllable (bīja) is the knower of the enemy's intent.
Therefore, having meditated upon the seed-syllable, whatever word one utters, that indeed shall be the mantra.
The practitioner wandering in the midst of the great darkness of ignorance attains the lamp of the oral instruction; whatever word he utters, that alone shall be the mantra. (63)
One need not recite the mantra from the *mālā*, nor must one accomplish the goddess through ritual procedures;
for one who knows the doctrine of Śrī Jvālinī, whatever word he speaks shall itself be the mantra. (64)

Even for one devoid of the worship of the Goddess, recitation, meditation, ritual performance, and fire-offerings, whatever word one who knows the Śrījvālinīmata utters shall itself be the mantra. (65)
Having understood the Vinaya, the Piṇḍa, O Goddess, the fivefold reality along with cessation, and the core of the instruction, whatever word one speaks, that indeed shall be the mantra. (66)

“Oṃ rkṣmlvyuṃ jvālāmālinī kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣoṃ kṣaṃ kṣaḥ hāḥ! Paralyze the evil planets! ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ! Hāṃ āṃ kroṃ kṣīṃ—Jvālāmālinī commands: huṃ phaṭ ghe ghe! Through instruction comes the efficacy of mantra; what can be accomplished by mantras devoid of instruction? Mantra, such as that of Jvālāmālinī and others, is effective when it is recited according to the ritual manual (kalpa). // 67 //
One should not write down in a book the mantra that has been received from ear to ear;
rather, it is obtained from the mouth of the Guru, as stated in the Śrījvālinīkalpa. (68)
A brief description of the seed-syllables:

[The syllable] *māṃ* is joined with the two forms of the Trimūrti and the letter *iṃ*; *māṃ* is situated in the ocean together with *iṃ*. *Māṃ* is the liquefier of the female seed (*retas*), while *mumā* is the moon residing in the heart; *drāṃ* and *drīṃ* are the two forms of Indrāṇī. // 69 //

The void (the letter *a*) joined with the second vowel (*i*) and the bindu; another [syllable] consisting of the second vowel (*i*) with the bindu; the lion-king (*ha*), the earth (*la*), the eye (*i*), and the cutter (*kṣa*)—this is the peak-syllable (*kūṭa*). With Viṣṇu (*u*) and the bindu, that would not be the reality (*tattva*). // 70 //

Āṃ Āṃ Kṣaḥ Iṃ Aṃ. [This is] the peak-syllable (kūṭa) situated within the seed-syllable (piṇḍa), upon a pericarp fashioned from non-seed-syllables, possessing sixteen vowels as its radiant filaments and the remaining seed-syllables as its eight petals.

One should meditate upon Jvālinī, the bestower of fruits, who dwells within the lotus encircled by the nine principles (tattvas) in the radiant [heart], and whose splendor is like that of a flame. // 71 //
At the navel, *klīṃ*; at the heart, *hrīṃ*; at the head, *dreṃ*; at the feet, *kṣīṃ*; at the anus, *drāṃ*;
on the crown of the head, *kroṃ*; *m* obstructed by *kuśa*; *madho ryyūṃ* above; *blūṃ* at the throat;
*yyūṃ* at the knees; *rathatena* obstructed; the stainless noose (*pāśa*) and the sound (*svana*) at the ears.
One should place the syllable *rū* in the ears, the word *śabda* in the throat, and the syllable *ka* in the body; then, one should place the supreme *bhūta* in the creation.
Oṃ hrīṃ; the four *rephas*, followed by *śikhimati* (the letter *śa*), ending with *vāṇa* (the letter *pa*), then *maḥ*;
the *piṇḍa* [mantra] thus formed is the essence (*tatva*) consisting of five excellent [syllables], followed by water twice (*ja-la-jala*) and that which blazes (*tat-prajvalan*).
Blazing! *Hraṃ* twice, *da-da* twice, and the pair *mā-ma*—[this is] the one who makes darkness from smoke (*dhūmāndhakāriṇī*).
"Make me quickly subject; this is clearly the mantra of Vaśaddevī. (74)

Oṃ hrīṃ hrāṃ hraṃ hrauṃ hraḥ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ, O Water, Water, Blaze, Blaze! Huṃ huṃ! Give me! O Dhūmāndhakāriṇī, come quickly and bring [the person named] so-and-so under my control! By means of the five deities of the egg (aja-piṇḍa), the five arrows, one's own five principles (tattva), and the words that restrain one's own desired object, the mantra-practitioner conquers all planetary influences. // 75 //

*Kṣalvyruṃṃ jvālāmālini drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ hāḥ! Paralyze all evil planetary influences! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ! Hā Āṃ Kroṃ Kṣīṃ! It performs pacification, enrichment, subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, killing, and expulsion. // 76 //
The Vinaya, together with the Jvālāmālinī, endowed with the nine principles, and the salutation—this Jvālinī-kalpa, along with its ritual offerings, is to be known today. // 77 //

The Vinayādi deity, the ninefold essence of the *piṇḍa*, conjoined with cessation (*nirodha*) and emptiness (*śūnya*), the seed-syllables for subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*), and the jewel-knowledge (*maṇividyā*). // 78 //

*jvālāmālini kṣalvyrūṃ hlavyrūṃ bhalvyrūṃ malvyrūṃ yalvyrūṃ palvṛyrūṃ ghalvyrūṃ, jhalvyrūṃ, ravlvyrūṃ ramlvyruṃ chamlvryūṃ kabhlvyrūṃ valvyūṃ / oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ drāṃ drīṃ hrīṃ āṃ hāṃ āṃ kroṃ kṣoṃ hāḥ vaṣaṭ saṃvauṣaṭ ghe ghe.* One should place the heart-mantra, the subsidiary-heart mantra, and the seed-syllables upon the little finger and the other fingers. Above that, one should recite: *oṃ jvālini janavaśyaṃ kuru kuru vaṣaṭ*, which is this essential truth (*tatva*). (79)

"Oṃ jvālāmālini, bring all people under my control, vaṣaṭ! By performing this common rite, one should wrap one's own arm with thread consecrated by the mantra held in the left hand, and thus bring people under control.
With the Bhīmakara [mantra], they two performed ten terrifying rites and the fire oblation.

"Let the mantra-practitioner not perform the ritual procedures of mantra-recitation, fire-oblation, observance, and meditation"—even if this were appropriate here, nevertheless, let him abandon the practice of the true mantra. (81)
First, can a single fire, when fanned by the wind, not accomplish anything?
First, can a single mantra, when joined with recitation and burnt offerings, have anything that is unattainable for it? (82)

Therefore, let the wise person perform here the ritual for propitiating the mantra according to the prescribed rules; if he is constantly free from laziness, he will attain the success he desires. 83.

The wise one should construct the common mandala in either a house for the deceased, on a crossroads, in the middle of a village, or in a region within a country; or on a plot of ground outside the city. // 1 //
Facing northeast, on level ground cleared of fallen water and debris, one should prepare an excellent mandala measuring eight cubits and divided into nine sections. // 2 //
One should draw a vast mandala with powders of five excellent colors, provided with four gates;
one should make it adorned with various banners, flags, mirrors, and bells. // 3 //

It was provided with an archway fashioned from *aśvattha* leaves and a pavilion for the Tatpuruṣa [form], with full jars placed upon the tips of pestles situated in all the intermediate directions. // 4 //

Having sprinkled that [ground], the wise man should draw within the eight auspicious squares the figures of Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, and Īśāna, endowed with their characteristic marks.
Śakra is yellow; Vahni resembles fire; the King of Death (Yama) is considered black;
Nairṛta is green; another [Varuṇa] has the luster of the moon; and Vāyu is dark-bodied.

One should draw all of them in sequence: Dhanada, who is multicolored; Śitabhairava; and Īśāna, whose vehicle is an elephant, a ram, a buffalo, a corpse, a crocodile, a rising deer, a horse, a bull, and a goat.
Having drawn [the deities] holding a vajra, fire, a staff, a spear, a sword, a noose, a great horse, a sickle, and a trident,
one should draw the Mother in the center of the world-protectors.

One should worship all [the deities] with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and so forth, using their respective mantras. This is declared to be the general maṇḍala for the expulsion of spirits. // 9 //

O guardians of the world, you who are the very doors of my self, please arrange these twelve types of mantras—two, one, one, one, two, one, and one—in due order within the directions starting from the east. 10.

The wise have declared that one's own mantras consist of the sequence ending with the oblation (*homānta*), including the two bindings (*dvirbandha*), fragrance, flowers, incense, lamp, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), the sacrificial offering (*bali*), and the cooked oblation (*caruka*). // 11 //
