The *Sarvatobhadra* Maṇḍala.
With three lines, each touching the tip of the other, and using five colors,
one should draw a square mandala measuring eight cubits in extent.
One should draw two lines in each of the four cardinal directions with a measurement of half that [length];
when this is done, there will be six points in the cardinal directions and four in the intermediate directions.
Then, one should write the group of Mother-goddesses (mātṛkā) in the inner eight compartments located in the cardinal directions;
they should be depicted together with their respective vehicles, faces, and weapons, while the remaining compartments are for the attendants.
The description of the group of eight Mothers: Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Aindrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī; these Mothers are white. (15)
Excellent ruby, moon-bearer (pearl), coral, blue lotus, sapphire, great royal mountain (emerald), and the color of the rising sun and the swan—these [colors] follow in sequence. 16.
The peacock, bull, and swan, as well as the eagle, boar, elephant, ghost, and mouse—these are declared by the wise to be the excellent vehicles of these [goddesses]. (17)

The lotus, the water-pot, the trident, the fruit, the gesture of granting boons, the fly-whisk, the discus, then the spear, the two nooses, the thunderbolt, the skull-cup, the lamp, and the axe—these are the weapons. (18)
The eight Daṇḍakarī goddesses, along with their respective attendants, are Vijayā, Vijayāpyā, Ajitā, Aparājitā, Gaurī, Gāndhārī, Rākṣasī, and Manoharī; these are the Daṇḍakarīs. (19)

In the outer eight directions and the corners, one should draw those world-protectors, Indra and the others, mounted upon their respective vehicles and bearing their own characteristic weapons and colors. // 20 //
Then, in the compartments situated on both sides of those two, [he visualizes] Indra and the other world-protectors, as well as Megha, Mahāmegha, Jvāla, Lola, Kāla, and Sthitanīla. // 21 //
One should draw the sixteen gatekeepers: Raudra, Atiraudra, Sajala, Jala, Himaka, Himācala, and likewise Lulita; and two Mahākālas each, as well as the two gatekeepers Nandi and [Mahānandi]. // 22 //
Outside, one should again construct a fourfold pavilion above with beautiful flowers;
one should fashion archways, garlands, mirrors, bells, and banners. // 23 //

One should install, according to the prescribed rite, white-colored jars filled to the brim and smeared with excellent seeds, honey, sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken grains, placed upon pestles situated at the corners.
Having drawn and installed a living being in the center of the mandala, and another made of clay elsewhere,
one should likewise place them in the center of the mandala and in the corners starting from the southeast, in successive order.
One should construct triangular sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), as well as pits surrounded by lotuses and water-pots;
these should be filled with the charcoal of the Khadira tree, the charcoal of Aṅgāraka, oil, and pure water. // 26 //
The application of this yantra is as follows:
having written the name of the planet surrounded by the syllable *ra* upon a leaf, one should place it within the heart of a figure made of flour or wax. // 27 //
Furthermore, having separately painted the form of the Graha on a leaf and on a cloth,
the wise one should write the cluster of the letter *ra* at the true joints of the form.
One should fill the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) [with fuel], cook the effigy (puttalikā) in a pot (kamallikā),
fasten the leaf to the waist, and heat the cloth within the pit.
Constantly reciting the mantras for the fire sacrifice at the monastery, when his suppressions were thwarted, he wailed bitterly, "I am burning! I am being burned! I am killed! (30)
For seven days or three days, for the sake of attaining renown and gain in the world, the mantra-practitioner should cause the planetary circle to turn back at his own will with great speed. (31)
On the seventh day after [the first], on the third day during the day, having caused him to dance in this great Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala according to the ritual procedure, || 32 ||
Then, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, or on the lunar day corresponding to that [deity], when Mars is rising,
one who knows [the rite] should dismiss the knower of the [mantra] during a difficult planetary configuration or an inauspicious ascendant.
One should draw a vast eight-petalled lotus as the maṇḍala of the pledge (samaya), using five-colored powders;
one should then draw a wide maṇḍala with four corners using colored powder. // 34 //
The faces of deer, boars, horses, elephants, bulls, buffaloes, cranes, and cats;
fruits, the gesture of granting boons, and swans—these, along with ornaments and auspicious marks, belong to women. 35.
One should draw the beautiful form in sequence upon the eight petals starting from the east;
in the center of that, having drawn a six-cornered fire-abode, one should depict the Fire-god.

Having written the syllables *yāṃ yīṃ yūṃ yauṃ* joined with the *repha* (the letter *r*) above and below, and likewise *yaṃ yaḥ*, in the middle of the squares starting from the east, one should place the left [syllable] at their tips.
One should draw the syllables *ryyūṃ* within the center of the hexagon and also within its internal compartments;
the planet is clearly to be seized in this [mandala] known as the Samayamaṇḍala. // 38 //
Having properly drawn a square with three lines using powder of five colors as before, one should then draw Śiva in the center of that mandala.
In the inner sections of the *satyamaṇḍala*, one should draw the deities beginning with Jayā in the compartments situated in the cardinal directions;
and those deities beginning with Gaurī in the compartments starting from the northeast (Īśāna). 40.
The first is Jayā, then Vijayā, as well as Ajitā and Aparājitā;
Gaurī, Gāndhārī, Rākṣasī, and Manoharī—these are the goddesses.
In the external northeast direction, one should write the letters beginning with *ka* in the various compartments starting from the square;
in this maṇḍala called Satya, the planet that is to be bound by oath must be made to speak the truth. 42.
One should draw Indra and the other world-protectors in the mandala starting from the eastern direction;
in the center, an image of an Arhat, and around it, deer facing one another. 43.
At the conclusion of this rite, one should display the incomparable maṇḍala of the universal assembly;
having bowed and offered praise, and having abandoned all enmity, one departs upon seeing this.

Thus [ends] the *Jvālāmālinīkalpa* from the work composed by the venerable Indranandimuni, which explains the meaning of that which was composed by the illustrious Helācārya; [this translation is] by Kāvya-sāhitya-tīrthācārya Prācyavidyāvaridhi Śrī Candraśekhara Śāstrī.
In the Bhāṣāṭīkā, the fourth chapter, titled "Maṇḍalādhikāra," is completed. // 4 //
The fifth chapter:
Bhūtākampana-taila;
Pūtika-śukatuṇḍikā, indeed Śukatuṇḍikā, and Tuṇḍikā as well.
Sita-kiṇī, hikkāśva-gandhā, bhū, kūṣmāṇḍī, and indravāruṇikā. // 1 //
Pūtikā, damanaka, ugragandhā, śrīparṇī, asakandha, kuṭaja, kukarañja, gośṛṅgī, śṛṅgī, nāga, sarpaviṣamuṣṭikā, and jīrakas. // 2 //
Nālī, rutccakrāṅgī, kharakarṇī, gokṣura, viṣa, nakulī, kanaka, varāhyā, hollā, asthipramathā, and lañjarikā. (3)
Pāṭalā, Kāmamadanataru, Vibhītaka tree, as well as Kākajaṅghā, Bandhyā, Devadāru, Bṛhatī, and secondly Sahadevī. // 4 //
Girikarṇikā, nadīmālikā, arka, śailārka, hastikarṇa, stunnimba, mahānimba, śirīṣa, lokeśvarī, and dāṇī; // 5 //
The *pāri* tree, the great tree, the pungent ones, and the roots used as necklaces;
the white and red *jāpā*, the foot of the *indravrāhma*, the two types of *kokilākṣa*, and lac. // 6 //
Bhṛṅga, devadālī, kaṭukaṃbī, and siṃhakeśara; ghoṣālikā, rkvabhakti, yati, muni, and the atimuktaka creeper. (7)
Bhagapuṣpī, nāgakeśara, śārdūlanakhī, and putrajīvī;
likewise śigru, eraṇḍa, tulasī, sadyas, and apāmārga. // 8 //

Having ground the ingredients with goat's urine mixed with the crushed testicles and eyes [of a goat], one should grind all these medicinal substances together with water from the cauldron of a leather-worker. // 9 //
Having divided [the mixture] into two parts and set aside one, the decoction is taken with urines;
in the case of *ardhāvarta*, one should stir the second part into the decoction. (10)
One should take equal parts of *kaṅgu*, *karuñja*, *raṇḍā*, *kolla*, *vibhītaka*, the two types of *nimba*, and sesame oil, and add them to the decoction while it is still boiling. (11)
In a house inhabited by spirits, on a day presided over by spirits, beneath a pavilion constructed from earth-born materials,
and when Mars is rising with its own degrees, one begins to cook.

One should thoroughly cook [the substance] with cow-dung and the rays of the sun fallen upon it, using fire produced from *khadira*, *karañja*, *arka*, *śamī*, and *nimba* fuel-sticks in great abundance. (13)
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the infusion of the limbs) upon one's own body with the seed-syllables *kṣipa*, *oṃ*, and *svāhā*,
one should perform the sakalīkriyā of the cook using those very same seed-mantras.

"Kṣipa oṃ svāhā. With this mantra, the practitioner of spells (mantrī) should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in a hearth provided with fuel, using all types of grain, mustard seeds, salt, and ghee, until the cooking is complete. He should perform the sacrifice with this homa-mantra. || 15 ||
Having reached a state of being devoid of moisture, just as water on dry ground becomes [evaporated], so too is the Bhūtākaṃpana oil prepared when it has undergone gentle heating. // 16 //

Asafoetida, realgar, bamboo manna, cinnamon bark, cardamom, yellow orpiment, the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper), the two types of turmeric, mustard seeds, garlic, rudrākṣa, coriander, and vacā; // 17 //
Ajamoda, the five salts, mārīṣṭaphala, udadhiphala, and trivṛt—
these should be added at each stage of cooking, along with castor oil.
Afterwards, the mantra-practitioner should consecrate the swords with the Rāvaṇa-vidyā mantra one thousand times; by this procedure, they will become perfectly accomplished.
Śākinīs, apasmāras, piśācas, bhūtas, and grahas are destroyed;
even potent poison becomes non-toxic through the application of this oil as an ointment or by inhalation.
Thus, in this work composed by the venerable Indranandimuni on the meaning of the *Śrīhelācāryapraṇītārtha*,
[is contained] the *Jvālāmālinīkalpa*, prepared by Kāvya-sāhitya-tīrthācārya Prācyavidyāvaridhi Śrī Candraśekhara Śāstrī.
In the Bhāṣā-ṭīkā, the fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bhūtākampa Oil," is completed. // 5 //
Now begins the sixth chapter, titled "The All-Protecting Machine," consisting of the mantra *āveṣṭya-sakāra-sānta-la-pa-glauṃ-yugma-pūrṇedubhiḥ*.
It is surrounded by divine syllables ending in *kṣma*, and encircled by those ending in *ra* located in the corners.
Outside, there is a sixteen-petaled lotus; then, the vowels are to be placed upon its petals.
In the corners is the syllable *kṣmā*, accompanied by the lords of the directions situated in the cardinal points, and on the outside is the mandala of earth.
This protective diagram (*yantra*), when inscribed with fragrant substances, removes the affliction of disease, untimely death, and the fear of malevolent planets and *piśācas*. (2)
One should draw the *yaṃtra* that protects from planetary influences and bestows sons, which consists of the syllable *Haṃ*, surrounded by all the vowels,
encircled by the earth-maṇḍala, and inscribed with the desired name outside of it; having drawn this, one should bow down to it with devotion.
The letter *va*, endowed with sixteen pure digits (*kalās*), is surrounded by the lunar mandala;
it is encircled by the letter *ya* joined with the vowels, and further enveloped by the solar orb joined with the vowels. // 3 //
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus; on each petal, one should inscribe the mantra ending with "namaḥ," followed by "pāśa-gajendra-varā-homa."
The seven oceans are outside, joined with the vowels,
encircled by the letter *ya*, and surrounded by the triad of winds.
"Oṃ āṃ śaṃ ña ṭha da dvi kalādya ja māśṛkā nahaṃ svāhā"—
this mantra called *Mṛtyujit* (Conqueror of Death), when written with fine saffron and other pigments,
should be worn on one's neck, arm, or garment; for him who wears it, there shall be no fear in this world.
The *kuṭhārī* protects from the ocean of nectar, rivers, thieves, untimely death, and worldly existence;
the *yudha* protects from *śākinīs* and hosts of planetary spirits (*graha*); and the *vandhyā* grants three sons. // 5 //
The *vaśya* (subjugation) yantra consists of the name surrounded by the letters beginning with *ṣa* and ending with *ha*, encircled by the three forms (*trimūrti*);
outside of this is a ring bearing the name of the eminent Kirāta, and further out is an eight-petaled lotus with double [the usual number of] petals.

The sixteen auspicious kalās are written upon the petals, encircled by the vowels excluding the head (the letter *ha*); moreover, it is surrounded externally by the three forms (*trimūrti*) and encircled by the letters beginning with *aja* (the letter *ka*).

Having inscribed this [mantra] upon a birch bark leaf with saffron, camphor, agallochum, musk, yellow pigment (rocanā), and other substances, one should worship it; this brings all under one's control. // 7 //
The *mohana-vaśya* yantra contains the name situated within the interior of *hari*; it is surrounded by the three forms of Rudra (*rudra-trimūrti*),
enclosed by the nine-syllable mantra (*navakāra*) as its casing, and encircled by the vowels ending in *ṭ*.

On the petals of the eight external lotuses, one should write the invocation of Jambha and the others, [beginning with] "O Jaya," followed by "Moha-mohaya amuka-naraṃ vaśyaṃ kuru svāhā" (Delude, delude such-and-such a man; make him subject, svāhā). 8.

One should write *kroṃ* at the tip of the petals; within that interval, one should write *hrīṃ hrīṃ*; on the exterior, one should write the mantra *śrāṃ śrīṃ śrūṃ* repeated twice; and outside of that, the word *śroṃ śraḥ*.
One should write this yantra, known as *mohana-vaśya*, upon birch bark (*bhūrja*) and worship it;
mixed with the juice of the *dhattūra* plant and fragrant substances, it becomes a means of enchantment (*mohana*). (9)

Aye jaye, delude, delude such-and-such a man; bring him under control, bring him under control! Vaṣaṭ! Aye jambhe, delude, delude such-and-such a man... [as above]... Aye vijaye, delude, delude... [as above]... Vaṣaṭ!
O Māhī, delude, delude!
O Ajitā, delude, delude! O Stambhā, delude, delude!

*O Aparājite! Delude, delude such-and-such a man! Make him subject, make him subject! Vaṣaṭ!* *O Staṃbhinī! Delude, delude!* [Vaṣaṭ] One should write *Kroṃ* on the tip of the petal, and immediately following that, one should write *Hrīṃ Hrīṃ* on the exterior.
Having inscribed this yantra, known as Mohana-vaśya, upon birch bark and worshipped it with fragrant substances mixed with the juice of the dhattūra plant, it shall become a means of enchantment.

Śrāṃ śṛīṃ śrūṃ śroṃ śraḥ; for the *strī-ākarṣaṇa* (attraction of women) yantra, one should write the name situated in the center of HRĪṂ, and KROṂ in each of the cardinal directions. One should also place the syllable YAṂ in those same directions.
On the outside is the svastika mark, the city of Śikhin, surrounded on the exterior by the letter Ra.
Outside that is a mass of fire, the triple-formed enclosure of fire; the city of Agni is surrounded by fire-piṇḍas, and beyond that, the fire-maṇḍala is encircled by hooks (aṅkuśas).
Outside, one should draw the excellent mandala of the goddess accompanied by the mantra;
then, it is encircled by three winds—this is the yantra, the most supreme in the world.

One should always perform the act of attraction by writing [the mantra] on birch bark with sandalwood, guru, saffron, moistened with buffalo-bile, camphor, gorocanā, musk, and other such substances. // 11 //
Having well-prepared lac and earth as a true counter-measure, place this *tapas* yantra together with a leaf inscribed with the name; fill it with lac with devotion,
and protect it with the thorns of the supreme *kṣa* syllable on the womb, the forehead, and the heart.
Having buried one [line] at the base of the pit, and having bound the other with its tip above the pit. // 12 //

At the two junctions of the day (saṃdhyā), one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with lac, guggulu, black mustard, sesame, and ghee, combined with salt and the name [of the target] written on a vessel.

By offering oblations for seven nights with the mantra of the deity of the netherworld (Atala), one can even bring Indrāṇī here; what need is there to mention the summoning of a woman dwelling on earth?

Having written the names of the "Divyagatisenā-jihvā-krodhastambhana-yantṛ" (the tongue-stupifying machine of the divine army of wrath), it should be placed inside a copper vessel, wrapped with four threads,
pierced by vajras at its extremities, and positioned within the opening of a thunderbolt, with the seed-syllable *vāṃ* at its tip.
The vajra is indeed mutually pierced; it is drawn above, surrounded three times by Viṣṇu.
That is the light with the lunar dot (bindu); in the syllable *la*, there is the pillar-dot of Hari and Kamalajaya.
A stone casket inscribed with the *tāla* [mantra] is wrapped and bound with yellow thread;
when worship has been performed, it paralyzes the army of the divine *gatis* and the tongue of the wrathful one. 15.
Having drawn a yantra for immobilization (*stambhana*) consisting of nine lines in the form of a vajra, thereby forming sixty-four squares;
on the outside, one should write the three bodies (*trideha*) with a dot (*bindu*), and inside that, the letter *la* with its final consonant (*liṃtasya vāntaḥ*) written without the dental *da*.

One should place the syllable *glauṃ* as the name within the womb; then, having enclosed it with a pair of thunderbolts (*vajra*) in the cardinal directions, one should encircle the interior of the thunderbolts with a ring using its own mantra on the outside.
The binding mantra is:

“Oṃ vajrakrodhāya jvāla jvālāmālini hrīṃ jhīṃ blūṃ drāṃ drīṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hauṃ hraḥ, destroy, burn, cook, and annihilate the anger, movement, mind, and tongue of Devadatta; O supreme one of wrath, svāhā! Having drawn this yantra on the ground, a plank, a wall, or a cloth with lac (tāla), [one should perform the rite].
One should honor with mantras that which has been worshipped, [thereby achieving] the paralysis desired by the heart. // 17 //
Having placed the syllable *la* in the corners of the yantra named Tongue-Paralyzer (*jihvā-stambhana*), it is surrounded by the ocean and the boat of the bindu;
it is encircled by the seed-syllables *laṃ*, *baṃ*, and *vaṃ*, and further enveloped by the threefold vajra-girdle.
Then, having written [the mantra] on birch bark with yellow pigment and saffron, one should take clay from the hands of a preeminent potter,
fashion a figure, and place that vessel in its mouth.

Having made that curved mouth formidable with a mass of armor-like feathers, he fixed his arrows within it; then, having properly applied the *jaṃbhana* [paralyzing] spell, he joined it with the *mohinī* [deluding] mantra.

Having worshipped with beautiful yellow flowers while reciting the mantra-syllable "svāhā," the man who departs [with this practice] conquers litigants who are his adversaries and paralyzes their tongues. 19.
Having written the names of the *yantras*— Gati, Jihvā, and Krodha— within the opening of the human mouth, surrounded by the letters from *ta* to *sa*;
then, with *lān*, *glauṃ*, and *tri* encircling the body, the seed-syllable is situated in the corner region.

The syllable *kṣīṃ* situated in the directions, the surface of the earth, and the tongue that is bent down—when the tongue is paralyzed by this mantra, it spreads delusion; thus the tongue, when restrained, effects the paralyzing of anger. (20) "Oṃ kṣi kṣīṃ."
"Oṃ jihvāstambhinī kṣiṃ kṣīṃ svāhā.
Having ground together rice, turmeric, and chalk, this yantra should be drawn with that paste upon a stone; when placed there, it brings about the desired success. (21)
Outside, one should draw the *puruṣavaśyayantra* and the goddesses Gaurī, Aparājitā, Vijayā, Jambhā, Mohā, Jayā,
Vārāhī, and Ajitā in sequence, starting from the left, with the seed-syllables *jrūṃ* and *saḥ* at their feet.

At the time of sexual union between a woman and a man, having carefully caught with a cotton cloth the organ that has fallen into the womb, one should avoid the ground and place it [upon a clean spot]. // 22 //

"Oṃ gaurīyai svāhā," "Oṃ aparājitāyai svāhā," "Oṃ vijayāyai svāhā," "Oṃ jṛmbhāyai svāhā," "Oṃ mohāyai svāhā," "Oṃ jayāyai svāhā," "Oṃ vārāhyai svāhā," "Oṃ ajitāyai svāhā," "Oṃ jrūṃ saḥ. Having inscribed this yantra on a birch leaf with saffron, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and other substances;
Having covered it with barley meal, one should scatter upon it the white powder of *kokilākṣa* seeds. // 23 //
That powder, mixed with water and semen, when applied as a paste and bound around the waist with a thread,
makes even a man who is naturally devoted to his own wife become a eunuch toward the wives of others.
In the center of the Kaṇayavaśya yantra, the name [of the target] is written twice, enclosed by the syllable Hrīṃ within the city of fire (the triangle).
In its squares, one should write "Vāma," "Hrīṃ Jaṃbhe Homa," and again "Vinaya. Furthermore, for the purpose of delusion (moha), one should write "Hrīṃ" and "Ca Homa. // 25 //

Then, in the intermediate spaces between those squares, one should write the seed-syllable that subdues elephants; outside of that, one should write "hrīṃ" interspersed with one's own name, and then on the exterior, one should write "śrūṃ" interspersed with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya).

With saffron, vermilion, honey, sandalwood, lac, cow’s milk, yellow pigment (rocanā), agallochum, and musk, one should draw this excellent diagram in the form of the universe with a golden stylus: "Oṃ hrīṃ jaṃbhe svāhā" and "Oṃ hrīṃ mohe svāhā. (27)
The yantra for removing the fear of śākinīs. // 1 //
Within the *oṃkāra* of the celestial vault (*nāka*), there is again a circle of sixteen *svastikas*; then the fire-house with nine flames rising, surrounded by the three *kalās*.
One should place the four cities of the Lord of the Immortals for this Fire, and the mantras situated in the intermediate spaces.
One should not steal this yantra inscribed by the three sons, for fear of the Śākinīs and out of dread. // 28 //
For the eastern direction:
"Oṃ vajradhare bandha bandha vajrapāśena sarvamaduṣṭavināyakānām oṃ hrūṃ kṣaṃ phaṭ yogine devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa svāhā."
In the south: “Oṃ amṛtadhare dhara dhara viśuddhe oṃ hrūṃ phaṭ yogini devadattaṃ rakṣa2 svāhā.
In the west:
“Oṃ amṛtadhare ḍākinī garbhasurakṣiṇī ātmabīja hrūṃ phaṭ yoginī devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa svāhā!
The northern [mantra] is: “Oṃ ru ru cale hrāṃ hnāṃ hrūṃ hrauṃ hraḥ kṣmāṃ kṣmīṃ kṣmūṃ kṣmaiṃ kṣmaḥ sarvayoginī devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa svāhā!”

The vessel-machine (ghaṭayantra) is surrounded internally by the ocean [of vowels] ending in *sakāra*, and externally it is encircled by the digits (*kalā*). It is to be enveloped by the eight [spirals] beginning with wind, and the syllable *haṃsa* forms the enclosure.

It should be encircled externally with the letter *ṭāṃ*; then the seed-syllables *kroṃ*, *proṃ*, *trīṃ*, and *ṭhaḥ* form a surrounding circle (*valaya*). It is well-encased on both sides by the letter *bhāṃ*, and that [mantra] is further encircled by the nectar-mantra (*amṛtamantra*). // 30 //
"Ṭha, kroṃ, proṃ, trīṃ, ṭhaḥ" | Oṃ pakṣi svaḥ jhvīṃ jvaṃ hūḥ vaṃ kṣaḥ haḥ haṃsaḥ jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ pakṣi svāhā | kṣaḥ saṃḥ saḥ hara huṃ hṛḥ | This is the Amṛta-mantra. // 31 //
The nectar mantra: "Oṃ pakṣi svaḥ jhvīṃ jvaṃ hūḥ vaṃ kṣaḥ haḥ haṃsaḥ jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ pakṣi svāhā / kṣaḥ saṃḥ saḥ hara huṃ hṛḥ.
The face, together with its lotus-petals, is surrounded on the outside by a jar of nectar at its base.
One should write "vaṃ" on the petals of the salutation and "laṃ" situated within the base petal.
Having drawn this jar-mechanism at the base of the immovable pillar upon a birch leaf, using saffron, yellow pigment, agallochum, camphor, sandalwood, lac, and milk; 33.
Having first wrapped it with thread and then encased it in beeswax,
the wise man should place it in a new full jar that has been honored with sandalwood, flowers, and other offerings.
The mantra for removing all obstacles is as follows:

the name, placed in the center of a double enclosure (sampuṭa) surrounded by the syllables ending in *ṭ* and *ṇ*, should be encircled by the syllables ending in *ś* and *v*. It should then be encircled by the syllables ending in *ṭ* and *bh*, and the word *haṃsaḥ* should form the outer circle (*valaya*). // 35 //
One should provide an outer circle of nectar-mantras and a sixteen-petaled lotus joined with the vowels;
one should write this mantra at the base of the jar using chalk, snow, and sandalwood paste.
“Oṃ amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaṃ srāvaya 2 saṃ 2 klīṃ 2 blūṃ 2 drāṃ 2 drīṃ 2 drāvaya drāvaya svāhā.
This is the Amṛta mantra;
having purified the surface of the ground, one should place a tripod made of iron upon it.
That flask’s opening must be covered with a lid made of bell-metal. // 37 //

A pestle joined with two waist-bands, washed with water, fresh, and adorned with a lattice of sandalwood paste, wrapped in most fragrant flowers, should be placed upon the top of that [vessel]. // 38 //
Having placed a lamp upon the pestle and a vessel made of bell-metal upon the base of the jar,
one should worship it externally with incense, perfumes, unbroken grains, flowers, sacrificial porridge (caru), and other offerings.

It instantly removes here the fear of cruel enemies, malevolent spirits (māra), female sorceresses (śākinī), serpents, the nine planets, piśācas, and thieves; for whoever prepares it with water as the constituent substance.
Having placed one's own name separately within the center of the *kūṭākāśapiṇḍa* of the *ākarṣaṇa*-yantra,
it should be surrounded by the *bhapiṇḍa*, the *parasatpiṇḍa*, and the secret [mantra].
On the outside, on eight-petalled lotuses, one should write another set of eight *piṇḍas* separated by petals; on the remaining eight petals, one should write pairs of vowels.

Below the pair of vowels, having placed the syllable *śabdam*, the noose (*pāśam*), likewise the *kuśam* and *kṣīṃ*, one should assign to them, in sequence, the first of those [syllables]: *hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *blūṃ*, *saḥ*, *drāṃ*, and *drīṃ*.
One should write the arrows— *hrāṃ āṃ kroṃ kṣīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ drāṃ auḥ drīṃ*— within the petals of the lotus, as well as the word *kaśaṃ* and the goad (*aṅkuśa*).
One should write *kṣīṃ* at the tip of each petal, and then [the mantra] ending with *namaḥ*, starting from the left (*vāmādi*).
Quickly draw that [seed-syllable] situated on the tip of the leaf with the arrow-point;
remain, O twice-born one, O speaker of truth, O giver of boons—having thus surrounded it on the outside with the mantra. // 43 //
Oṃ hrāṃ āṃ kroṃ kṣīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ drāṃ drīṃ, O Goddess Jvālāmālinī, quickly summon Devadatta! Stay, stay! Homage to you, O speaker of truth, O granter of boons! //43//
Outside the *yantra* of the supreme deity and the *graha*s, one should write *hrīṃ* encircling the head; then, having formed three lines extending from that,
one should write *klīṃ* in the center, *drāṃ* and *drīṃ* in the pair of upper corners, and *blūṃ* below.
Outside, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, draw a city with the seed-syllable *raṃ* and the earth-syllable (*laṃ*) combined;
outside of that, draw the ocean, marked with the syllables *vaṃ*, *digva*, *digā*, *tala*, and *kāra*.

The Goddess Jvālāmālinī said: "O Lord, this planetary yantra should be drawn on birch bark or even on a tablet during the Puṣya asterism, under the sun, and according to auspicious ritual procedures. (45)

When the *vaśya-havana* is performed with the mantra of the Heart and Sub-Heart of Śikhimaddevī, and when it is constantly worshipped, recited, and offered as oblations, it brings all women, kings, enemies, and the elements under one's control. // 46 //

One should offer ten thousand oblations with the three sweets mixed with guggulu incense and the ten-ingredient and five-ingredient incenses; this brings even Indra under one's control, so what need be said of others?
Thus, in this work composed by the venerable Indranandimuni on the meaning of that which was authored by the illustrious Helācārya,
this is the *Jvālāmālinīkalpa*, prepared by Kāvya-sāhitya-tīrthācārya Prācyavidyāvaridhi Śrī Candraśekhara Śāstrī.
In the Bhāṣāṭīkā, the sixth chapter, titled "The Section on Vaśya Yantras," is completed. // 6 //
Now begins the seventh chapter:
The Tilaka for Subjugating All;
[the ingredients are] śarapuṃkhī, sahadevī, tulasī, musk, and camphor.
Gaurī-rocana, elephant ichor, realgar, and likewise damanaka. // 1 //
Take equal parts of *jāti*, *śamī* flowers, and *harikāntā*; this divine formulation, when used as a forehead mark (*tilaka*), brings the world under one's control. // 2 //
For the *tilaka* and *añjana* that bring the world under one's control:
cardamom, cloves, sandalwood, *tagara*, blue lotus, costus, saffron, *uśīra*, white *rocanā*, *keśara*, realgar, black mustard, and *kuṭaja*. (3)
One should take equal parts of *hikvā*, *tulasī*, and *padmaka*, and at the rising of the moon, a maiden should grind the whole mixture with water from a silver vessel.
One should apply a tilaka with this [mantra], or likewise apply collyrium to one another;
the tilaka is that which makes one the ornament of the three worlds, made from elephant-ichor, *kunaṭī*, and *śamī* flowers.
A forehead mark (*tilaka*) made from all these—
*narakanda*, leaf-juice, *kanyā*, snow-lotus, blue lotus, beautiful filaments, *kuṣṭha*, *harikāntā*, and sandalwood— is a transformative mark that brings the world under one's control. // 6 //

A forehead mark (*tilaka*) made from equal parts of sesame seeds for subjugation, *kanakasahajātā* flowers, jasmine, and musk, when applied, brings the people of the three worlds under one's control. (7)
Mukhasaugandhika, Karatila, Pāvakavarjitā, Lakṣmī, Sahadevī, Kṛṣṇā, Mallikā, Tulasī,
Harikāntā, Narakaṇḍeśvarī, Śītā, Uśīra, and Piṅkā. // 8 //
A pair of *jāti* and *śamī* flowers, *damanaka*, yellow *guarocanā*, and *apāmārga*;
saffron, *kāryyaka*, musk, *dhatūra*, and leaves of the *maruka* tree. // 9 //
With the shafts of reeds and *kanaka* taken in equal parts, combined with divine, auspicious threads and joined with flower-stalks, there shall be a face-covering ornament known as a *tilaka*.

For the purpose of subjugating all, [the ingredients are]: collyrium, iron dust, *śarapuṅkhā*, *sahadevī*, *mohinī*, *mayūraśikhā*, saffron, *kuṣṭha*, sandalwood, camphor, and the flower of the *śamī* tree. // 11 //
Rājāvarta, bhrāmaka, divasakara, āvarta, madajaṭā, māṃsī, nṛpapūlikā, īśa, candana, bālā, girikarṇikā, and śvetā [are the ingredients]. (12)
Srotoñjana, nīlāñjana, sauvīrāñjana, and rasāñjana;
also padmāhi, siṃhakeshara, śārdūlanakha, and vikṛta. (13)
Having scattered the powder of gaurī-rocana, aśvavandana, harikāntā, bhṛṅga, and tuttha upon a layer of lac, and having wrapped it, one should fashion a wick. 14.
One should visualize her as being encircled by a five-colored thread with the milky sap of trees;
furthermore, one should correctly visualize her again with the milk from the breasts of a compassionate woman. 15.
Having kindled a lamp at a consecrated site with cow’s ghee using a wick, one should apply as an ointment to the eyes the crushed seeds of *dhatura* that have been ground together. 16.
Reciting the mantra "Oṃ hariṇī hariṇī svāhā," one should apply collyrium; or, while reciting that very same mantra, one may also prepare eye-salve. (17)
O fortunate one, you spread this collyrium that delights the entire world;
your two devoted eyes bring women, men, and kings under your control. 18.
The devotees of the bliss-bestowing collyrium— Bhrāmaka, Himāñjana, Nīlāñjana, Bālā, Lakṣmī, Sumohinī,
Vyāghranakhī, Harikāntā, and Varakanda— along with Rocanā [should be used]. (19)

Having written "kekikhe" upon these layers of lac-dye and having ground them together according to the previously mentioned procedure, this is that which both pleases people and yet does not please them. 20.
The collyrium that bestows all happiness consists of *harikāntā*, *kekiśikhā*, *śarapuṃkhī*, *pūtikeśa*, *sahadevī*,
*himamada*, *rājāvarta*, *vikṛti*, *kanyā*, and *puruṣakanda*. (21)
This powder, prepared from equal parts of *puruṣadamana* and *keśara*, combined with *pāmodhinī* according to the previously mentioned procedure, is an elixir that enchants the entire world. // 22 //

This collyrium, which bestows happiness, consists of tiger-claw, deluding blue collyrium, enchanting camphor, and combined with yellow pigment (gaurī-rocanā); when applied according to the prescribed rite, it brings delight to the world. // 23 //

For the purpose of bringing all under one's control (*sarvavaśīkaraṇa*), the collyrium consists of saffron (*kāśmīrakuṣṭha*), sandalwood (*malayaja*), the filaments of the *kamala* and *utpala* lotuses, *sahadevī*,
*bhrāmakanyā*, *nṛpaharikāntā*, *vikṛti*, and *mayūraśikhā*. (24)
Camphor, yellow orpiment, *mohinī*, blue collyrium, and saffron—this collyrium, prepared according to the previously mentioned procedure, brings the entire world under one's control. (25)
Regarding the practice for subjugation (vaśyaprayoga):

black sesame seeds should be soaked separately for three days with the juice of castor seeds (*eraṇḍaka*) and the milk and urine of a female dog; these are the arrows of the Conqueror of the Body (Anaṅgajaya). // 26 //
Having prepared many pills from vaśyā, namaka, red kaṇavīra, vīkṛti, dvijadaṃṣṭrī, vāruṇī, bhujaṅgākṣī, lañjarikā, and govaṃdinī, [he administered them]. 27.
Having added salt along with the pills into a fine vessel and having infused them with one's own urine, one should cook it afterwards; this salt brings the world under control. (28)
For the *vaśya-taila* (subjugation oil), one should take fifteen, nine, four, and six parts of the substance called *vikṛti-mohana*.
Having understood [the requirements for] the *lañjarikās*, one should prepare it on the new moon day during a Saturday. (29)
Having ground half a *kalka* with goat’s milk, one should boil it with that goat’s milk;
when the decoction is reduced by half, one should add a second portion to it. // 30 //
One should cook oil double the quantity of honey, mixed with an equal amount of decoction, according to the prescribed method;
this "Madanābhyañjana" oil for women brings the three worlds under one's control.
For the subjugating oil (2):
having placed the leaves of *kramuka* fruits into one's own dead body for comfort, one should place it in a secluded and auspicious location, smeared with cow dung in its midst. // 32 //
Having taken those [ingredients] and placed them within a golden vessel with a fine lid over three days,
one should treat them with the powders of *girikarṇikā*, *indravāruṇī*, *nalada*, and *halinī*.

One should repeatedly process [the substance] with the milk of the *mandāra* flower along with its own urine; this should be done slowly on a Saturday at the time of the *kulika* [astrological conjunction], while [the substance] is placed upon a fire fueled by gold. (34)
Guñjā, sugandhikā, and the powder of kanakabīja, when fumigated with snake-shaped figures using sesame oil, become the weapons of Anaṅga through the opening of a vessel. (35)
For subjugation (*vaśya*),
[one should use] the powders of *gobandhinī*, *indravāruṇī*, *avanīdaraka*, *karṇikā*, *sugandhikā*, and *kharakarṇī*, together with pieces of betel nut. (36)

Those [drugs] contained in the vessel of the madwoman should be processed separately with one's own urine, with red oleander, with the juice of the *dragharā* plant, and with the milk from the breast of a female dog. (37)
The weapons of the Flower-Arrowed One were well-anointed with the oils of unmatta, bīja, guñjā, sugandhika, sarpa, kṛtita, and tila,
and heated over a fire of golden fuel.
Regarding the application for subjugation (vaśyaprayoga):

one should take the powder of *kanyā*, *elavāluka*, *nāga*, *sarpa*, *pātāla*, *garuḍa*, and *rudrajaṭā*, combined with *kramuka* fruits and one's own excrement, [to be applied] upon a large golden fruit. 39.
"Having honored the weapons of Manojas that had been soaked in dog's milk and then thoroughly fumigated, they shall be victorious," thus was it said by his preceptor, the Lord of the Gaṅgā.
Having placed the powder of *kāmabāṇa*, *rudrajaṭā*, white *guñjā*, and *lañjarikā* into the mouth of a snake,
one should take it after three days and reduce it to a fine powder, mixing it with one's own excrement.
Having smeared the root of the *hari* plant with cow dung and meditated upon it, one should cook it according to the prescribed rite;
this powder, known as the "Arrow of Desire," brings the entire world under one's control. // 42 //
An external pill [prepared from] the powder of *daśarārika*, *kanaka*, *indravāruṇī*, *kharakarṇikā*, *trisandhyā*, *visphoṭana*, *nalajjarikā*, *dvija*, and *daṇḍī*. (43)
Having placed them in a vessel, one should separately add black pepper, salt, mustard seeds, ginger,
powdered *dhānyājamoda*, yellow myrobalan, betel nut, and long pepper.

These ten, known by the names of the enemies, who bring the entire world under their control, are to be properly cultivated with their own impurities and separately perfumed with their respective incenses. (45)
One may freely apply a paste of *yoniśodha*, *dhātaka*, elephant ichor, *kuṣṭha*, musk, camphor, *unmatta*, *pippalī*, *kāma*,
*rudrajaṭā*, honey, rock salt, ginger, *mustā*, and *yaṣṭī*. (46)
A paste composed of surana, ṭaṅkaṇa, pippalī, śarapuṃkhī, mātuluṅga, and a heap of caṇaka, combined with mahākāmla, causes the destruction of the vulva when applied. 47.
One should prepare a desired preparation of long pepper combined with camphor, cardamom, honey, and *lajjārikā*, along with milk and *kuraṇṭikā*, which will conquer the female organ. 48.
The life-prolonging medicinal herbs are śipha,
phaṇīphala, cavya, citraka, mahī, kuśmāṇḍī, niḥparṇikā, brāhmī, dūrvā, pūrvikā, mitā, varāhā, kā, and khalvā.
If one grinds pāṭhā and lakṣmaṇikā with the milk of a black cow and administers it, even a barren woman who has begun to menstruate will certainly obtain a son together with her husband. (49)
Having both remained for four days after drinking this nectar-like medicine,
they should eat sweet food in a secluded place once their task is completed.

Having bathed on the fourth day and having fulfilled her husband’s resolve, she who has bowed to Śiva and lies down on her right side shall obtain a daughter, while she who lies on her left side shall obtain a son.

Thus [ends] the *Jvālāmālinīkalpa* from the work composed by the venerable Indranandimuni, which explains the meaning of that which was composed by the illustrious Helācārya; [this translation is] by Kāvya-sāhitya-tīrthācārya Prācyavidyāvaridhi Śrī Candraśekhara Śāstrī.
In the Bhāṣā-ṭīkā, the seventh chapter, titled "The Section on Subjugation" (Vaśyādhikāra), is completed. // 7 //
Now begins the eighth chapter:
the ritual procedure for the bathing ceremony of Vasudhārā; [it should be performed] in a delightful and pure location, facing the northeast, provided with a water vessel.
It should be thoroughly cleansed with the dung of a tawny cow, as well as curd, milk, ghee, and urine. // 1 //

Having written the name together with the digit of the full moon in the center, one should surround it on the outside with the flowers of the kokanada, kumuda, kuvalaya, raktotpala, and other aquatic blossoms. // 2 //
It was joined by pairs of swans from the lakes of Cakrāhva, Balabālāka, and Sārasa;
it was filled with waves where crabs, tortoises, frogs, crocodiles, and sea-monsters frolicked. // 3 //
One should draw a vast cluster of lotuses with powder of five colors;
outside of that, one should likewise delineate a square mandala according to the prescribed rule.
In the corners, having placed white-colored full jars adorned with gold, decorated with sandalwood, saffron, and flowers, and topped with excellent *bījapūra* fruits; // 5 //
Having constructed a pavilion for virtuous persons above that, one should tie a jar with nine holes made in its center, suspended in the middle of it.
Having inscribed the diagram known as Mṛtyuñjaya together with the names upon a birch leaf,
one should wrap it in beeswax, enclose it along with gold, and deposit it within the water-pot.
Mṛtsadevī, saumyākṣī, kṣīrataru, bark, suvarṇa, harikāntā, ripe uśīra, haridrā, dūrvā, kāśmīra, and flowers. // 8 //
Having ground together these— jasmine, agallochum, and sandalwood— with water,
one should consecrate each with fifteen mantras in successive order.
Having raised up that Devadatta by means of a single reversal,
one should fashion a single effigy from those very stones fallen upon the ground.
One should have divine images made from perfected clay, representing the foremost guardians of the eight directions, joined with their respective lineages and endowed with the [auspicious] marks.

The definition of perfected clay: clay found at the king’s gate, at a crossroads, from a potter’s workshop, from *āmalūra* plants, on both banks of a river, or from the tusks of elephants and the horns of bulls taken from a field, is perfected. // 12 //
Black, yellow, red, dark blue, green, moon-white, black, multicolored, and white—these are the offerings of cooked rice (caruka) endowed with fragrances and other such substances. // 13 //
Having offered nine cloths, one should place the image of Māla in the first [cell];
in the remaining [cells], one should install the images of Indra and the others in successive order. // 14 //
Furthermore, having drawn a mandala outside in a certain place as before, one should first bathe that Devadatta there with warm water. (15)
Then, for the common worship, there is the Vinaya mantra accompanied by Jvālāmālinī: *atha hūṃ yugaṃ*, then *sarvān apamṛtyūn*, *dvighātaṃ saṃ vaṃ maṃ devadatta*, and then the pair *atha rakṣa*. (16)
Reciting the mantra "Śāntiṃ kuru kuru sadvaruṇāṃ devate nija baliṃ ca gṛhṇa yugaṃ svāhā," one should increase [the effect] with an offering of cooked rice mixed with impurities. // 17 //
Oṃ jvālāmālini huṃ huṃ, destroy all deaths! Saṃ vaṃ maṃ, protect Devadatta! Perform peace, perform peace! O noble Varuṇa deity, accept your own offering! Svāhā! // 17 //
Having thus increased the *caru* with the mantra, one should cast it into the river;
one should also increase the *carus* for the guardians of the directions with their own respective mantras:
"Oṃ kūṭa piṇḍa śikhinī saṃ vaṃ maṃ haṃ ca [for] Devadatta."
Bestow peace, contentment, and nourishment; protect the pair and the couple. // 19 //
"O Goddess of the Directions, accept this offering"—with this mantra, one should perform the rites up to the end of the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Having thus completed the ritual according to the procedure, one should cast the offering (*bali*) into the midst of the water with the utterance "Svadhā. (20)

Oṃ kṣmlvryūṃ jvālāmālini saṃ vaṃ maṃ haṃ, grant peace, satisfaction, and nourishment to Devadatta; protect, protect! O deity of the direction, accept this offering, svāhā! This is the mantra for increasing the prosperity of the eight guardians of the directions: Oṃ kṣmlvryūṃ jvālāmālini saṃ vaṃ maṃ haṃ, grant peace, satisfaction, and nourishment to Devadatta; protect, protect! O deity of the direction, accept this offering, svāhā!
Having adorned his body with divine garments, ornaments, flowers, sandalwood paste,
and the like, and having risen from that spot, let him proceed mounted upon the sandals of the planet.
With his hands joined in añjali at his forehead and holding flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata), he circumambulated that maṇḍala and then sat down facing it in its center.

The Vasudhārā mantra: “Oṃ vasudhāradevate jvālāmālini jala jala vijala vijala sujala sujala hema hema śītala śītala devi! O Goddess who possesses the rays of ten million suns and moons, act! Hūṃ! O you who cause the agitation of the three worlds! Kṣā kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ! O Goddess, together with your own retinue of deities, quickly grant satisfaction and nourishment to Devadatta! Bestow the increase of the glory of the True Dharma, strength, long life, health, and sovereignty! Destroy all calamities and great fears! Strike down all untimely deaths!”

"Quickly protect! May the nine planets, all situated in the eleven houses, become givers of fruit: *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hrauṃ hraḥ svāhā*. Make everything subject: *krauṃ krauṃ vaṃ maṃ haṃ saṃ taṃ svāhā*. Reciting this *Vasudhārā* mantra, one should offer water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), cow urine, the five products of the cow (*gavya*), buttermilk, curd, the three sweets, and likewise milk. (23)
Having also poured the water from five excellent sprouts into a hanging jar and placed it below that [image], one should thereafter offer scented water. // 24 //
One should place images of the nine planets made of flour and endowed with a golden color upon the sacrificial pap (caru) mentioned by oneself, as previously described. // 25 //
The Sun and Mars are red; Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are yellow; Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu are white; and they are black in color. (26)

One should offer oblations of sacrificial rice (caru) in sequence, accompanied by excellent sandalwood paste, unbroken grains, flowers, radiant lamps, and incense, while reciting this mantra. // 27 //
The mantra for the nine planets is:

*Oṃ jvālāmālini sarvābharaṇabhūṣite glauṃ glauṃ haklauṃ haklauṃ klīṃ klīṃ la la la la sarvamṛtyūn hana hana trāsaya trāsaya hūṃ hūṃ kṣūṃ kṣūṃ haṃsaḥ phaṭ ghe ghe sarvarogān daha daha hana hana śīghraṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa navagraha devate baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa ghe svāhā*. Having thus increased [the power], one should cast that *caru* into the middle of a river.
The bathing circle arising from the bath [is performed] with the mantra accompanied by the *varaṇa* (offering). // 28 //
After the bath, the garments, ornaments, jewel-pitchers, and so forth, should not be given to anyone else; they should be taken by oneself as being suitable for one's own use. // 29 //
Having given her other garments, ornaments, and so forth to clothe and adorn her, he should afterwards go elsewhere to a clean place that has been swept and provided with a fourfold seat. // 30 //
Thereafter, let him bind upon the neck of this Devadatta the knowledge of Mṛtyuñjaya, which instantly removes disease and death. (31)

Having offered [the cloth] according to the ritual procedure, covered with a washed white cloth and a yellow silk scarf, the mantra-practitioner should bathe [the image] with a bath consisting of a rain of exceedingly fragrant flowers. 32.
The primary bath:
*Oṃ kroṃ jvālāmālini hrīṃ klīṃ llūṃ drāṃ drīṃ hrāṃ ām kroṃ kṣīṃ devadattaṃ sugandhapuṣpasnānena sarvaśāntiṃ kuru2 vaṣaṭ*. This is the mantra for the shower of flowers bath.
Thus, for Devadatta who has been bathed according to this rite, [there appears] the goddess Śikhimatī.
It always bestows glory, fragrance, health, contentment, and nourishment. // 33 //
It increases longevity, removes the affliction of planetary influences, destroys the fear of enemies, annihilates millions of obstacles, and pacifies many kinds of diseases. // 34 //
Let this rite called Vasudhārā, spoken by Jvālāmālinī, which destroys all untimely death and is prescribed according to the ritual for pacification, be performed.
Thus, in this work composed by the venerable Indranandimuni on the meaning of the treatise authored by Śrī Helācārya,
[is contained] the *Jvālāmālinīkalpa*, translated by Kāvya-sāhitya-tīrthācārya Prācyavidyāvaridhi Śrī Candraśekhara Śāstrī.
In the Bhāṣāṭīkā, the eighth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Vasudhārā Bath," is hereby completed. // 8 //
Now begins the ninth chapter:
One should have [images] fashioned from flour that has been kneaded for the rite of lustration (nīrājana), incorporating all the colors.
The faces of the eight excellent Mother-goddesses, together with their ornaments. // 1 //

One should offer [the oblation] daily according to the prescribed rite, using each individual mouth [of the vessel] accompanied by many kinds of food, sacrificial porridge, lotuses, sacrificial flowers, unbroken grains, lamps, and incense. // 2 //

One should bind the power within the Mātṛkā using mantras produced from the *piṇḍa* [syllables] ending in *kū*, *ū*, *kā*, *nta*, *bhā*, *nta*, *ṭha*, *kāra*, *ambu*, and *sā*; at the end of the mantra, one should say: "Seize, seize me, HŪM! (3).
Even each individual [ingredient], when increased, becomes a remover of many defects for men;
having thus increased them, one should offer that bali-oblation in the midst of water. // 4 //
Kālī, Mahākālī, Mālinī, and likewise Kaṅkālī; Satkāla, Rākṣasī, Varajaṅghā, and Śrījvālinī—these indeed [are the goddesses]. // 5 //
Having fashioned the faces of these divine deities—Vikarālī, Vaitālī, and the others—endowed with their characteristic marks, using high-quality prepared clay; ||| 6 ||
With sharp claws and the tips of fangs, eyes wide and rolling, and tongues lolling out;
they were provided with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, sandalwood paste, lamps, incense, and many kinds of food.
One should perform the *nivardhanaka* rite day by day, increasing it one by one,
beginning on the fourteenth day for nine days until the seventh.

Having performed the lustration rite (*nīrājana*) which brings about prosperity and destroys inauspiciousness, the pure practitioner, reciting the mantra "mukharipu" one hundred times, should offer that sacrificial oblation (*bali*) into the midst of the water. // 9 //
Vīreśvara, Āśavaṭuka, the great leader of obstacles Pañcaśiras,
and Kāla— these faces should be fashioned from flour.
Fierce, endowed with three eyes, with radiant lamps placed upon their heads, and accompanied by many offerings of food, flowers, sandalwood, fragrant incense, and so forth. // 11 //

By increasing that single [offering] with the "Moon-Face Enemy" mantra (*mukhendravairi-mantra*), the bali offering, when thrown into water, removes the afflictions of planetary influences, diseases, and epidemics. (12)

Having prepared that [offering] with well-kneaded rice cooked in milk, mixed with curd and ghee, one attains the form of Vāgīśvarī, who possesses difficult-to-subdue teeth and fangs, and is perfectly accomplished. 13.
One should offer a brilliantly burning lamp upon the head of the wick of the perfected one (siddhavarti);
furthermore, one should cause the eight tongues of the eyes to perform [the recitation] one hundred and eight times.
With that form, accompanied by parched grain, incense, bright fragrant flowers, garlands, and perfumed smoke, one should perform the rite of increase at night, which removes all defects.
One should fashion the form of Vāgīśvarī from ground [clay], possessing sharp, high, white fangs, a flickering tongue, and three eyes that destroy fear; she is most formidable. (16)

With that form, accompanied by many offerings of food, sacrificial porridge, lamps, and incense, one should perform the rite of nourishment (*nivardhana*) which removes all defects, using the sword-mantra (*khaḍgamantra*). // 17 //
Yoginikā, Divyamahāyoginikā, Yoginī by means of the perfected mantra, Anyujaneśvarī, Pretāvāsinī, and the goddess Śākinī. (18)
One should have the sacrificial offerings (balis), carus, and foodstuffs made from flour mixed with these [substances].
One should fashion eight tongues and one hundred and eight eyes as previously described. (19)
With a bell, a small vessel, and garlands of lamps, perform daily the rite of increase with each individual mantra according to its specific form. // 20 //
Taking a handful of rice grains, one should fashion the form of a planet, complete with its characteristic marks, on a surface [measuring] a number of years exceeding a human lifespan.
Having placed that form—provided with many offerings of food, perfumes, garlands, lamps, and incense—within the fire, nine small cloth bags were situated upon it. 22.
The mantra-practitioner, loudly reciting the Rāvaṇa-vidyā with the Khaḍga-mantra,
should first worship it with flowers and then strike the entrance of the house with rice grains.
Having increased the number of animals by that same amount according to the prescribed rite, one should offer the bali-oblation in the midst of water at night; this quickly removes all defects.
This "Nīrājanavidhi," as described by the goddess Jvālāmālinī, swiftly dispels the fear of planets, spirits, *śākinīs*, and untimely death. // 25 //

Thus, in this work composed by the venerable Indranandimuni based on the meaning of the *Jvālāmālinīkalpa* authored by the illustrious Helācārya, [this is] the contribution of Kāvya-sāhitya-tīrthācārya Prācyavidyāvaridhi Śrī Candraśekhara Śāstrī.
In the Bhāṣā-ṭīkā, the ninth chapter, titled "Nīrājana-vidhi," has been completed. // 9 //
Now begins the tenth chapter:
the procedure for bestowing knowledge upon the disciple.
In a location within a temple of the Jina that is empty and provided with water falling from the northeast direction—
In a delightful place, swept clean with cow dung and cow urine that have not fallen [to the ground]. // 1 //
With five-colored powder, one should draw a square mandala according to the prescribed rite, measuring one cubit on each side, marked with three lines and known as "Truth."

Outside of that, in the midst of the waters of the western direction, one should draw the form of Varuṇa, filled with aquatic creatures and surrounded by the delusive whirlpools of river currents. // 3 //
One should place full jars, adorned with sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, their openings covered with citron fruits and containing gold, at each of its four corners.
One should have a pair of feet made of gold or silver for the Goddess;
having consecrated them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as with curd, ghee, excellent milk, and fragrant waters. // 5 //
Having placed the pair of feet worshipped in the southern region of the mandala,
one should draw the two subsequent pairs of feet in the directions beginning with the south-west (nairṛti).

Having drawn the pair of lotus-feet of the Arhat in the center of the mandala with colored powder, one should write the pairs of feet of the Siddhas, the Sun, the Teacher, and the Muni in the corners. // 7 //
One should worship everything with perfumes, unbroken grains, flowers, excellent lamps, incense, and cooked rice;
above that, one should construct a charming pavilion adorned with various kinds of flowers. // 8 //

Having thus drawn the mandala with truth, one should afterwards worship the feet of the Guru with fragrant substances, flowers, and so forth, as well as with bracelets, earrings, garments, and other ornaments.

Having wrapped the book with threads of gems, gold, and silver, and with divine cloths, and having placed it at the pair of feet of the goddess Śikhinī, one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings. 10.

With his hands joined in a cupped añjali at the forehead holding flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata), having performed circumambulation and entered the center of the mandala, the disciple should be bathed with water from the jars.
Such bathing, clothing, ornaments, and so forth are appropriate for the disciple; they are not intended for anyone other than the Guru.
After he has put it on, another garment or similar item should be given to him. // 12 //
Knowledge and so forth should be given to that person who bows at the feet of the Goddess, the sages, and the Guru, who is endowed with devotion to the true Dharma, and who holds a book. // 13 //

You should not give these regions to one devoted to other doctrines, but to a person of dharma who is devoted to your own doctrine, endowed with discipline toward the guru, and whose mind is always moist with compassion. (14)
Whatever sin may arise from the killing of a sage, a cow, a woman, or others—if you give [this] to another sect, it will be yours as well; having been told this, it should be given. // 15 //

Having clearly made the earth, water, wind, fire, the sacrificer, space, the moon, the sun, and so forth, together with the hosts of planets and stars, his witnesses, one should give [the gift]. // 16 //
"Having called upon you, me, the goddess Śikhinadā, the teacher Helā, and the world-protectors as witnesses, she says: 'This [gift] is indeed given by me to you. (17)

The vidyā should be given by the disciple according to the ritual of accomplishment (sādhana-vidhi); it should be given by the disciple according to the ritual of accomplishment. The vidyā should be received according to the ritual; that disciple shall become one who has mastered the vidyā. // 18 //

Victorious is the Sage Helācārya, the Lord of Jinas, who is preeminent in the time of the poetic composition of the Samayas, who is perfected in the practice of discerning the path, and who is protected by the vows, the restraints, and the guards. // 19 //
Thus, for as long as the earth, oceans, moon, sky, stars, and principal mountains endure, may one remain steadfast in the meaning of the teachings spoken by the Master in the Śrījvālinīkalpa. 20.

Thus [ends] the *Jvālāmālinī-kalpa*, from the work composed by the venerable Indranandimuni on the meaning of that which was composed by the illustrious Helācārya; translated by Kāvya-sāhitya-tīrthācārya Prācyavidyāvaridhi Śrī Candraśekhara Śāstrī.
In the Bhāṣāṭīkā, the tenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Accomplishment" (Sādhanavidhi), is completed. // 10 //
